nameStory: Common hawkweed gets its name from an ancient belief that hawks would eat this plant to sharpen their eyesight for hunting. Medieval herbalists thought the milky sap from hawkweeds could improve human vision too, though we now know this isn't true. The 'common' part simply means it's the most widespread of the hawkweeds.
description: Common hawkweed is a perennial wildflower that produces bright yellow, dandelion-like flowers on slender stems. The plant typically grows 1-3 feet tall with a rosette of hairy leaves at the base and smaller leaves climbing up the branched flowering stems. Like other members of the sunflower family, what looks like a single flower is actually a cluster of tiny individual flowers packed together in a flower head.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flower heads about 1 inch across, looking like small dandelions but carried on tall, branching stems rather than single stalks. The petals are actually ray flowers with squared-off, toothed tips that feel papery to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are covered in soft, whitish hairs that make them feel fuzzy and look grayish-green. Basal leaves form a rosette and are lance-shaped, while stem leaves are smaller and clasp the stem.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a branching plant 1-3 feet tall, unlike dandelions which have single flower stalks. Multiple flower heads branch out from the main stem in an open, airy pattern.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Stems are hairy and often have a reddish tinge, feeling rough and slightly sticky when you run your fingers along them. They branch near the top to hold multiple flower clusters.

habitat: Common hawkweed thrives in disturbed soils and open areas throughout New England, including roadsides, old fields, meadows, and forest clearings. It prefers well-drained soils and full sun to partial shade. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy species like goldenrod, asters, and other non-native plants in areas that have been cleared or disturbed.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge from the base in a fuzzy rosette, and flower stems begin to develop in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from June through August, when the bright yellow flowers are most abundant and easily spotted.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, then produce fluffy white seedheads similar to dandelions. Basal leaves may persist through mild weather.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back, but the root system survives underground to regrow next spring.

funFact: Common hawkweed is actually a botanical shapeshifter - it can reproduce both by seeds and by underground runners, and many hawkweed 'species' can hybridize so readily that botanists sometimes throw up their hands and call difficult-to-identify hawkweeds 'the Hieracium complex!'
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with dandelions, but remember that dandelions have single flowers on hollow stems rising directly from the ground, while hawkweeds have multiple flowers on branching, leafy stems. The hairy, grayish leaves of hawkweed also feel much fuzzier than dandelion's smooth, deeply-toothed leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Common hawkweed is native to Europe and is considered a weedy species that can crowd out native plants in some areas. While not as aggressive as some invasive plants, it's worth knowing that this cheerful yellow flower is actually a non-native addition to New England's landscape.
compareHints: Among the many hawkweed species in New England, common hawkweed is distinguished by its branching growth habit and grayish, hairy leaves. Rattlesnakeweed has distinctive purple-veined leaves, while Canada hawkweed has much narrower leaves that are nearly hairless underneath. Panicled hawkweed tends to be taller with more open, spreading flower clusters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Panicled hawkweed stands out from its hawkweed relatives by being much taller and more upright than species like rattlesnakeweed or spotted hawkweed.
Among its hawkweed relatives, rattlesnakeweed stands out for its ground-hugging rosette growth pattern and prominent leaf veining.
Rough hawkweed is much more bristly and hairy than its relatives like panicled hawkweed or Canada hawkweed, which have smoother stems and leaves.
Among New England's hawkweeds, this species stands out for its multi-branched flowering stems and medium height.
Among New England hawkweeds, Canada hawkweed stands out for its exceptionally narrow, smooth leaves and tall, elegant stature.
Among New England's hawkweeds, spotted hawkweed stands out for its tall, branching flower stems and tendency to grow in disturbed soils.
Among New England's hawkweeds, wall hawkweed is distinguished by its preference for rocky, vertical surfaces and its distinctly heart-shaped leaves with purple veining.
Among New England's hawkweeds, Beaked Hawkweed stands out for its extremely small flowers and very hairy lower stem.
Among its hawkweed relatives, Robinson's hawkweed stays much smaller than New England hawkweed or Canada hawkweed, which can grow much taller.
